\section{Introduction}

In 1913 Ramanujan sent Hardy a letter containing scores of formulas stated
without proof. The episode has become emblematic of mathematical intuition: a
faculty that appears to \emph{know} truths in advance of demonstration. It is
natural to ask whether such a faculty could be mechanized --- whether one could
program a device that reliably classifies mathematical statements as true or
false.

We call such a hypothetical device a \emph{Ramanujan oracle}. The original
motivating conjecture was that an oracle achieving high accuracy on
number-theoretic statements cannot be computable. We prove a clean and general
version of this claim by a counting argument, and then strengthen it in three
independent directions. The results are elementary in their tools ---
Cantor's theorem and the countability of programs --- but the layering into a
constructive form and an accuracy-theoretic form gives the impossibility real
teeth: it is not merely that a computable oracle fails to be perfect, but that
for any enumerable family of oracles there is a \emph{single explicit} world on
which \emph{every} member is wrong infinitely often and has accuracy zero.

\section{The model}

We fix an effective G\"odel numbering of mathematical statements, so that
statements are identified with the natural numbers.

\begin{definition}[Statement]
A \emph{statement} is a natural number $n \in \N$, understood as the G\"odel
code of a syntactic mathematical assertion.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Ground truth]
A \emph{ground truth} is a function $T : \N \to \{\text{false}, \text{true}\}$,
assigning to each statement its actual truth value. We write $\Truth$ for the
set of all ground truths; as a set it is $\{\text{false},
\text{true}\}^{\N}$, the set of infinite binary sequences.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Oracle]
An \emph{oracle} is a function $O : \N \to \{\text{true}, \text{false},
\unknown\}$, realized as $O : \N \to \mathsf{Option}(\{\text{false},
\text{true}\})$, with $\unknown$ modeled by the absent value. We write $\Oracle$
for the set of all oracles.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Correctness]
An oracle $O$ is \emph{correct} on statement $n$ with respect to ground truth
$T$ if $O(n) = \some\,(T(n))$. An $\unknown$ answer is never correct.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Perfection]
An oracle $O$ is \emph{perfect} for ground truth $T$, written $\Perfect(O, T)$,
if $\forall n \in \N,\; O(n) = \some\,(T(n))$.
\end{definition}

We allow oracles the third answer $\unknown$ precisely to be \emph{generous} to
the oracle-builder: the device is never forced into a wrong commitment. The
impossibility results hold despite this generosity, because hedging never counts
as correct and therefore never helps an oracle be perfect.

\section{The counting argument}

\begin{proposition}[Non-vacuity]\label{prop:nonvac}
For every ground truth $T$ there is an oracle perfect for $T$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take the echo oracle $O(n) := \some\,(T(n))$. Then $O(n) = \some\,(T(n))$ for
all $n$, so $O$ is perfect for $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uncountability of ground truths]\label{thm:uncountable}
The set $\Truth$ is uncountable; indeed $|\Truth| = 2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
As a set, $\Truth = \{\text{false}, \text{true}\}^{\N}$, whose cardinality is
$2^{\aleph_0}$. By Cantor's theorem $2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0$, so $\Truth$
cannot be injected into $\N$. Concretely, given any sequence $(T_k)_{k\in\N}$ of
ground truths, the diagonal truth $D(n) := \lnot\, T_n(n)$ differs from $T_k$ at
statement $k$ for every $k$, so no sequence enumerates all of $\Truth$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect oracles are world-determining]\label{thm:unique}
If $O$ is perfect for $T$ and also perfect for $T'$, then $T = T'$. Hence each
oracle is perfect for at most one ground truth.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For every $n$, $\some\,(T(n)) = O(n) = \some\,(T'(n))$, and injectivity of
$\some$ gives $T(n) = T'(n)$. As this holds for all $n$, $T = T'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Countable coverage]\label{lem:cov}
Let $\iota$ be a countable index set and $F : \iota \to \Oracle$. Then
$\Cov(F) := \{\, T \in \Truth \mid \exists i,\; \Perfect(F(i), T)\,\}$ is
countable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Define $g : \Cov(F) \to \iota$ by sending each covered world $T$ to some index
$i$ with $\Perfect(F(i), T)$. If $g(T) = g(T') = i$, both $T, T'$ are covered by
$F(i)$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:unique} $T = T'$; thus $g$ is injective. An
injection into the countable set $\iota$ makes $\Cov(F)$ countable.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uncountable miss]\label{thm:miss}
For any countable family $F : \iota \to \Oracle$, the set
$\Miss(F) := \{\, T \in \Truth \mid \forall i,\; \lnot\,\Perfect(F(i), T)\,\}$
is uncountable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\Miss(F) = \Cov(F)^{\complement}$. If $\Miss(F)$ were countable, then $\Truth =
\Cov(F) \cup \Miss(F)$ would be countable, contradicting
Theorem~\ref{thm:uncountable}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Incompleteness of countable families]\label{cor:incomplete}
For any countable family of oracles there is a ground truth $T$ such that no
oracle in the family is perfect for $T$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Non-computability}

\begin{theorem}[No computable oracle scheme is complete]\label{thm:scheme}
Let $F : \N \to \Oracle$ enumerate oracles produced by programs. There exists a
ground truth $T$ with $\lnot\,\Perfect(F(i), T)$ for all $i$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Immediate from Corollary~\ref{cor:incomplete}, since $\N$ is countable.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No universal oracle]\label{thm:universal}
There is no oracle $O$ that is perfect for every ground truth.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:incomplete} to the constant family equal to $O$; the
resulting world $T$ satisfies $\lnot\,\Perfect(O, T)$.
\end{proof}

Fix a standard theory of computation in which every computable function is
computed by a code (a natural number), and a code determines the function it
computes.

\begin{theorem}[Only countably many computable oracles]\label{thm:count-comp}
The type $\{\,O \in \Oracle \mid O \text{ is computable}\,\}$ is countable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each computable oracle $O$ is realized by some code $c$ computing $n \mapsto
\mathrm{encode}(O(n))$. Choose such a code $c(O)$ for each computable $O$. If
$c(O) = c(O')$ then the codes compute the same function, so
$\mathrm{encode}(O(n)) = \mathrm{encode}(O'(n))$ for all $n$; injectivity of the
encoding gives $O = O'$. Thus $O \mapsto c(O)$ injects into the countable set of
codes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Honest impossibility]\label{thm:honest}
There exists a single ground truth $T$ that defeats every computable oracle: for
every computable oracle $O$, $\lnot\,\Perfect(O, T)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:count-comp} the computable oracles form a countable family;
apply Corollary~\ref{cor:incomplete}.
\end{proof}

\section{Constructive strengthening: infinitely many errors}

\begin{definition}[Adversary]
For an oracle $O$, the \emph{adversarial world} $\adv(O) : \N \to \mathsf{Bool}$
is
\[
\adv(O)(n) := \begin{cases} \lnot b & \text{if } O(n) = \some\,b, \\ \text{true} & \text{if } O(n) = \unknown. \end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:adv}
$O$ is incorrect on every statement in $\adv(O)$: for all $n$,
$\lnot\,\Correct(O, \adv(O), n)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $O(n) = \some\,b$ then $\adv(O)(n) = \lnot b \ne b$, so $O(n) \ne
\some\,(\adv(O)(n))$. If $O(n) = \unknown$, then $O(n)$ is not of the form
$\some(\cdot)$, so it is not correct.
\end{proof}

Fix a computable pairing bijection $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle : \N^2 \to \N$
with inverse $n \mapsto (\pi_1 n, \pi_2 n)$.

\begin{definition}[Block-diagonal world]
For a family $F : \N \to \Oracle$, set $\mathrm{block}(F)(n) := \adv(F(\pi_1
n))(n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Block diagonalization]\label{thm:block}
For any family $F : \N \to \Oracle$ there is a single ground truth $T =
\mathrm{block}(F)$ such that for every $i$, $F(i)$ is incorrect at infinitely
many statements:
\[
\forall i,\quad \{\, n \mid \lnot\,\Correct(F(i), T, n)\,\} \text{ is infinite.}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $i$. For $n$ with $\pi_1 n = i$, $\mathrm{block}(F)(n) = \adv(F(i))(n)$, so
by Lemma~\ref{lem:adv} $F(i)$ is incorrect at $n$. Hence $\{ n : \pi_1 n = i\}
\subseteq \{ n : \lnot\,\Correct(F(i), T, n)\}$. The left set is infinite:
$j \mapsto \langle i, j\rangle$ injects into it. A superset of an infinite set
is infinite.
\end{proof}

\section{Accuracy: no guaranteed accuracy across all worlds}

\begin{definition}[Running hits]
For an oracle $O$, world $T$, and threshold $N$, let $\hits(O, T, N) := \big|
\{\, n < N \mid O(n) = \some\,(T(n))\,\} \big|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Zero hits against the adversary]\label{lem:zero}
For any oracle $O$ and every $N$, $\hits(O, \adv(O), N) = 0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:adv}, $O(n) \ne \some\,(\adv(O)(n))$ for every $n$, so the
filtered set is empty.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No guaranteed accuracy]\label{thm:acc}
There is no oracle $O$ with
\[
\forall T\ \forall N \ge 1, \quad 20 \cdot \hits(O, T, N) \ge 19 \cdot N,
\]
i.e.\ no oracle achieves accuracy $\ge 19/20 = 95\%$ in every world.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose such $O$ existed. Apply the hypothesis in the world $\adv(O)$ at $N =
1$: it demands $20 \cdot \hits(O, \adv(O), 1) \ge 19$. But by
Lemma~\ref{lem:zero} the left side is $0$, and $0 \ge 19$ is false.
\end{proof}

The constant $95\%$ plays no special role: the same proof refutes any fixed
positive accuracy threshold.

\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Where the impossibility bites.} The theorems forbid a \emph{program}
that is perfect \emph{simultaneously across all worlds}. They say nothing
against an oracle tailored to \emph{our} world, for which a perfect oracle
exists as an abstract object (Proposition~\ref{prop:nonvac}). The content is
that no uniform, enumerable rule captures the correct answer key, because that
key lives in an uncountable space while rules live in a countable one.

\textbf{Relation to undecidability.} The counting argument is orthogonal to the
classical undecidability of arithmetic truth: our result shows non-existence of
a universal oracle across all worlds, while the classical result shows that even
the single true arithmetic is undecidable.

\textbf{Relation to cryptography.} The gap exploited here --- countably many
programs against uncountably many possibilities --- mirrors the logic of
cryptographic hardness, where security rests on the chasm between the instances
an adversary can enumerate and the space it cannot.

\textbf{On the bounded-length framing.} A set of statements of length at most a
fixed bound is finite and hence trivially decidable by table lookup, so the
impossibility must be phrased over an unbounded supply of statements, as we do.

\section{Future directions}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Genuine recursion-theoretic computability} (realized here):
    phrase the result directly in terms of decidable predicates and oracle
    Turing machines with relativized queries.
  \item \textbf{Undecidability, not just non-computability}: encode the halting
    problem into the ground truth of a fixed world.
  \item \textbf{Quantitative accuracy over density}: obtain a world on which
    each oracle has upper error density bounded below by a positive constant.
  \item \textbf{Bounded-length statements}: replace a fixed bound by a growing
    family $S_k$ and study the degradation rate of computable accuracy.
  \item \textbf{Probabilistic oracles}: model an oracle as a distribution over
    verdicts and study expected accuracy across all worlds.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

A Ramanujan oracle guaranteed flawless across all possible mathematical worlds
cannot be computable. Perfect oracles determine their worlds, so a countable
supply of oracles pins down only countably many of the uncountably many possible
worlds. We upgraded this to the honest notion of computability, made the
adversarial worlds explicit through block diagonalization, and showed that no
fixed positive accuracy can be guaranteed across all worlds. Ramanujan's
intuition, on this reading, was not a universal oracle but a superb
world-specific heuristic --- and the counting argument explains why that is the
only kind of oracle that can exist.

from typing import Callable, List, Optional, Sequence

# A truth value world is a tuple of bits; an oracle answer is 0, 1, or None.
Truth = Sequence[int]

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Core predicates                                                             #

def correct(oracle: Oracle, truth: Truth, n: int) -> bool:
    """Correct(O, T, n): the oracle commits to the true verdict at n."""
    return oracle[n] is not None and oracle[n] == truth[n]


def perfect_on(oracle: Oracle, truth: Truth) -> bool:
    """Perfect(O, T): correct on every statement in the prefix."""
    return all(correct(oracle, truth, n) for n in range(len(truth)))


def echo_oracle(truth: Truth) -> Oracle:
    """The echo oracle O(n) = T(n); perfect for exactly this world."""
    return list(truth)


def adversary(oracle: Oracle) -> Truth:
    """The adversarial world: opposite of every committed answer.

    Where the oracle says None (unknown), we output 1 (any value works).
    Guarantees the oracle is correct on *no* statement.
    """
    return [(1 - a) if a is not None else 1 for a in oracle]


def hits(oracle: Oracle, truth: Truth, upto: int) -> int:
    """Number of correct commitments among the first `upto` statements."""
    return sum(1 for n in range(upto) if correct(oracle, truth, n))


def all_worlds(n: int) -> List[Truth]:
    """All 2^n possible ground truths on a prefix of length n."""
    return [list(bits) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=n)]

    print("=" * 68)

    world: List[int] = [0] * n
    for i in range(num_oracles):

    print("  -> every oracle errs on its entire block simultaneously.\n")

    print("  -> a universal oracle would need to cover all worlds; impossible.\n")

Numerical demonstrations for:

    Ramanujan Oracles Cannot Be Computable: A Counting Argument

We model the abstract objects of the paper over a finite prefix of statements
(the first N Goedel-numbered statements) so that everything is concrete and
computable:

    * A "ground truth"  T : N -> {0, 1}     (a world / answer key)
    * An "oracle"       O : N -> {0, 1, None}   (None = "unknown")
    * "Correct(O, T, n)"  iff  O[n] == T[n]  (a None answer is never correct)
    * "Perfect(O, T)"     iff  O is correct on every statement

The theorems illustrated:

    * exists_perfect_oracle   -- the echo oracle is perfect for its world.
    * perfect_unique          -- a perfect oracle determines its world uniquely.
    * counting mismatch       -- 2^N worlds vs. a countable list of oracles.
    * adversarial world       -- drives any oracle's accuracy to exactly 0.
    * block diagonalization   -- one world defeats a whole family at once.
    * no guaranteed accuracy  -- the adversary refutes any fixed accuracy bound.

Everything is self-contained; run `python demo.py`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Optional, Sequence

# A truth value world is a tuple of bits; an oracle answer is 0, 1, or None.
Truth = Sequence[int]
Oracle = Sequence[Optional[int]]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Core predicates                                                             #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def correct(oracle: Oracle, truth: Truth, n: int) -> bool:
    """Correct(O, T, n): the oracle commits to the true verdict at n."""
    return oracle[n] is not None and oracle[n] == truth[n]


def perfect_on(oracle: Oracle, truth: Truth) -> bool:
    """Perfect(O, T): correct on every statement in the prefix."""
    return all(correct(oracle, truth, n) for n in range(len(truth)))


def echo_oracle(truth: Truth) -> Oracle:
    """The echo oracle O(n) = T(n); perfect for exactly this world."""
    return list(truth)


def adversary(oracle: Oracle) -> Truth:
    """The adversarial world: opposite of every committed answer.

    Where the oracle says None (unknown), we output 1 (any value works).
    Guarantees the oracle is correct on *no* statement.
    """
    return [(1 - a) if a is not None else 1 for a in oracle]


def hits(oracle: Oracle, truth: Truth, upto: int) -> int:
    """Number of correct commitments among the first `upto` statements."""
    return sum(1 for n in range(upto) if correct(oracle, truth, n))


def all_worlds(n: int) -> List[Truth]:
    """All 2^n possible ground truths on a prefix of length n."""
    return [list(bits) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=n)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstrations                                                              #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def demo_perfect_unique(n: int = 4) -> None:
    """Each oracle is perfect for at most one world (perfect_unique)."""
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Demo 1: a perfect oracle determines its world uniquely")
    print("=" * 68)
    worlds = all_worlds(n)
    world = worlds[5]  # pick one world
    oracle = echo_oracle(world)
    matches = [w for w in worlds if perfect_on(oracle, w)]
    print(f"  prefix length n = {n},  #worlds = {len(worlds)}")
    print(f"  chosen world   = {world}")
    print(f"  echo oracle is perfect for exactly {len(matches)} world(s): {matches}")
    assert len(matches) == 1 and matches[0] == list(world)
    print("  -> confirmed: perfect for exactly one world.\n")


def demo_counting_mismatch(n: int = 6, num_oracles: int = 10) -> None:
    """A short list of oracles covers only a tiny fraction of worlds."""
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Demo 2: counting mismatch (few oracles cannot cover many worlds)")
    print("=" * 68)
    worlds = all_worlds(n)
    # A "countable family" modeled by the first `num_oracles` echo oracles.
    family: List[Oracle] = [echo_oracle(worlds[i]) for i in range(num_oracles)]
    covered = {tuple(w) for w in worlds if any(perfect_on(o, w) for o in family)}
    print(f"  #worlds (2^{n})       = {len(worlds)}")
    print(f"  #oracles in family    = {num_oracles}")
    print(f"  #worlds covered       = {len(covered)}  (<= #oracles)")
    print(f"  #worlds MISSED        = {len(worlds) - len(covered)}")
    assert len(covered) <= num_oracles
    print("  -> a finite/countable family covers <= (its size) worlds.\n")


def demo_adversary(n: int = 8) -> None:
    """The adversarial world drives an oracle's accuracy to 0 (no_accuracy)."""
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Demo 3: adversarial world -> accuracy identically zero")
    print("=" * 68)
    # An arbitrary (even partly "unknown") oracle.
    oracle: Oracle = [0, 1, None, 1, 0, None, 1, 0][:n]
    adv = adversary(oracle)
    print(f"  oracle           = {oracle}")
    print(f"  adversarial world= {adv}")
    for upto in range(1, n + 1):
        h = hits(oracle, adv, upto)
        print(f"    hits among first {upto}: {h}  (accuracy {h/upto:.0%})")
    assert all(hits(oracle, adv, upto) == 0 for upto in range(1, n + 1))
    print("  -> the 95% (or any positive) accuracy guarantee is refuted.\n")


def demo_block_diagonalization(block_size: int = 3, num_oracles: int = 4) -> None:
    """One world defeats an entire family at once (block diagonalization)."""
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Demo 4: block diagonalization defeats a whole family")
    print("=" * 68)
    n = block_size * num_oracles
    # Family of arbitrary oracles.
    family: List[Oracle] = [
        [(i + k) % 2 for k in range(n)] for i in range(num_oracles)
    ]
    # Block-diagonal world: on block i, play adversary against oracle i.
    world: List[int] = [0] * n
    for i in range(num_oracles):
        adv_i = adversary(family[i])
        for k in range(block_size):
            idx = i * block_size + k
            world[idx] = adv_i[idx]
    print(f"  n = {n}, {num_oracles} oracles, block size {block_size}")
    print(f"  block-diagonal world = {world}")
    for i, o in enumerate(family):
        block_idx = range(i * block_size, (i + 1) * block_size)
        errs = sum(1 for idx in block_idx if not correct(o, world, idx))
        print(f"    oracle {i}: wrong on {errs}/{block_size} of its own block")
        assert errs == block_size
    print("  -> every oracle errs on its entire block simultaneously.\n")


def demo_no_universal_oracle(n: int = 4) -> None:
    """No single oracle is perfect for every world (no_universal_oracle)."""
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Demo 5: no single oracle is perfect for every world")
    print("=" * 68)
    worlds = all_worlds(n)
    # Try any fixed oracle; count worlds it is perfect for.
    candidate: Oracle = [0] * n
    good = [w for w in worlds if perfect_on(candidate, w)]
    print(f"  candidate oracle = {candidate}")
    print(f"  perfect for {len(good)} of {len(worlds)} worlds; misses "
          f"{len(worlds) - len(good)}")
    assert len(good) < len(worlds)
    print("  -> a universal oracle would need to cover all worlds; impossible.\n")


def main() -> None:
    demo_perfect_unique()
    demo_counting_mismatch()
    demo_adversary()
    demo_block_diagonalization()
    demo_no_universal_oracle()
    print("All demonstrations completed and assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

| `|I|` | systems `I→Bool` | equivalence classes |
|-------|------------------|---------------------|
| 1     | 2                | each singleton (equality) |
| 2     | 4                | each singleton |
| n     | `2^n`            | `2^n` (equality) |

C(e₁)+C(e₂) = e₁⊗e₁ + e₂⊗e₂                                     (linearity)

# Future Directions — Lifebox: Information-Theoretic Identity

The file `LifeboxInformationIdentity.lean` formalizes and proves five claims around
Rudy Rucker's *Lifebox* thesis (identity = information, not substrate). Below: what was
established, and where it can be pushed.

## What was proved (all `sorry`-free, standard axioms only)

1. **Person-equivalence is an equivalence relation** and coincides with function equality
   (`personSetoid`, `personEquiv_iff_eq`).
2. **Finite-state ⇒ decidable.** For a finite stimulus space with decidable outputs,
   person-equivalence is decidable via the distinguishing-stimulus set
   (`decidablePersonEquiv`, `finiteState_decidable`).
3. **Contrarian result (disproof of a naive claim).** Over an infinite input space, *no*
   finite battery of tests certifies person-equivalence (`no_finite_test`). This shows the
   finiteness hypothesis in (2) is necessary, not cosmetic.
4. **Quantum obstruction = no-cloning.** There is no linear cloning map `k² → k² ⊗ k²`
   (`no_cloning`) — the algebraic core of the "quantum brains cannot be duplicated/tested"
   claim.
5. **Kolmogorov bound is finite.** Identities in `b` bits number exactly `2^b`
   (`card_identities`), specialized to Rucker's `~10^15`-bit figure (`lifebox_bound`).

## Directions to extend

- **Genuine automaton equivalence.** Upgrade (2) from "finite stimulus space" to full
  Moore/Mealy machines over `List I`, proving language equivalence decidable via the
  product-automaton reachability construction, with the Myhill–Nerode distinguishing-string
  bound `≤ |S₁|·|S₂|`.
- **Quantitative no-cloning.** Strengthen (4) to fidelity bounds: an approximate cloner has
  fidelity bounded away from 1, and generalize from `k²` to arbitrary `dim V ≥ 2` and to the
  unitary/CPTP setting.
- **Undecidability, formally.** Reduce the halting problem to equivalence of systems whose
  behaviour encodes Turing machines, giving a true `¬ Decidable` statement (rather than the
  "no finite test" surrogate) for the infinite/quantum regime.
- **Kolmogorov complexity proper.** Replace the counting bound with a `K`-style shortest
  description length over a fixed universal machine, and prove invariance and subadditivity
  (cf. the EML Kolmogorov development in `Catalog/EML/KolmogorovComplexityBound.lean`).
- **Substrate independence.** Formalize the Lifebox thesis directly: two systems on
  different state spaces that are behaviourally equivalent (bisimilar) are "the same person",
  i.e. person-identity factors through the behaviour quotient.
